Glasgow.region: Glasgow and the west of Scotland
Glasgow.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Glasgow and the Clyde
s1loc: Glasgow runs one of Scotland's largest visitor economies, drawing millions of trips a year. The marquee draws cluster along the Clyde and the West End, from the Zaha Hadid Riverside Museum and the Tall Ship Glenlee to Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, the country's most visited free attraction. Glasgow Cathedral, the Necropolis, the Gallery of Modern Art and the Glasgow Science Centre with its IMAX and Tower fill out the headline list.

The leisure and activity layer is just as busy. The OVO Hydro and the SEC Armadillo anchor the Scottish Event Campus, while Pollok Country Park, the Burrell Collection, the People's Palace on Glasgow Green and the Buchanan Galleries and Argyle Street shopping quarters keep visitors moving. Theatre Royal, the King's Theatre, Celtic Park and Hampden tours, plus the West End and the Merchant City festivals, give activity operators and event teams a long working season.

Heritage and hospitality round it out, from the Mackintosh trail and the Glasgow School of Art to the Tenement House and the Trades Hall. A deep city-centre hotel trade runs through the Merchant City, Finnieston and around George Square, supported by a wide tour-guide scene, Glasgow Central and Queen Street stations, the Subway and Glasgow Airport at Paisley drawing visitors in from the doorstep.

Edinburgh.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Edinburgh and the Lothians
s1loc: Edinburgh carries one of the UK's busiest visitor economies, drawing millions of trips a year. The marquee draws run along the Royal Mile from Edinburgh Castle, with its Crown Jewels and Stone of Destiny, down to the Palace of Holyroodhouse, taking in St Giles' Cathedral, the National Museum of Scotland, Camera Obscura and the Scott Monument. The Royal Yacht Britannia at Leith and Arthur's Seat in Holyrood Park complete the headline set.

The leisure and activity layer is just as busy. Princes Street Gardens, Dynamic Earth, Edinburgh Zoo and the Royal Botanic Garden draw families, while the Usher Hall, the Festival Theatre and the Playhouse run year-round. The August festivals, led by the Edinburgh Festival Fringe and the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo, plus Hogmanay and the Princes Street and St James Quarter shopping districts, keep activity operators and event teams working hard.

Heritage and hospitality round it out, from the Old Town and New Town World Heritage Site to Gladstone's Land, the Writers' Museum and the Georgian House. A deep hotel trade runs through the New Town, the Grassmarket and the Leith waterfront, supported by a wide tour-guide and ghost-walk scene, Waverley and Haymarket stations, the trams and Edinburgh Airport bringing visitors in from the doorstep.

Liverpool.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Liverpool and Merseyside
s1loc: Liverpool runs one of the country's biggest visitor economies, built around its waterfront. The marquee draws cluster at the Royal Albert Dock, from the Beatles Story and Tate Liverpool to the Merseyside Maritime Museum and the International Slavery Museum, with the Royal Liver Building, the Museum of Liverpool, the Liverpool Cathedral and the Metropolitan Cathedral close by along the Pier Head.

The leisure and activity layer is just as busy. Anfield and Goodison Park stadium tours, the M and S Bank Arena, Sefton Park and the Palm House, the World Museum and the Walker Art Gallery draw steady crowds, while the Liverpool ONE shopping quarter, the Cavern Club, the Royal Court and the Empire Theatre keep family attractions, activity operators and event teams busy across the year.

Heritage and hospitality round it out, from the Magical Mystery Tour and Penny Lane to Strawberry Field, Speke Hall and the Williamson Tunnels. A deep hotel trade runs through the Ropewalks and the Baltic Triangle, supported by a wide tour-operator and guide scene, the Mersey Ferries from the Pier Head, Lime Street station and Liverpool John Lennon Airport at Speke bringing visitors in from the doorstep.

Newcastle upon Tyne.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Tyneside
s1loc: Newcastle anchors a strong North East visitor economy along the Tyne. The marquee draws run across the Quayside, from the Tyne Bridge and the Gateshead Millennium Bridge to the Discovery Museum with Charles Parsons' Turbinia, the Great North Museum: Hancock, the Laing Art Gallery and St Nicholas' Cathedral, with the BALTIC Centre for Contemporary Art and the Glasshouse International Centre for Music on the south bank.

The leisure and activity layer is just as busy. The Utilita Arena, the Theatre Royal and the City Hall run year-round, while Leazes Park, Jesmond Dene, St James' Park stadium tours and the Eldon Square and Grainger Town shopping quarters draw steady footfall. Antony Gormley's Angel of the North just south, the Hoppings on the Town Moor and the Quayside markets keep activity operators and event teams working across the season.

Heritage and hospitality round it out, from Grainger Town and Grey Street to the Castle Keep, Bessie Surtees House and Segedunum Roman Fort at Wallsend. A deep hotel trade runs through the city centre and the Quayside, supported by a wide tour-guide scene, Newcastle Central station, the Tyne and Wear Metro and Newcastle Airport at Woolsington bringing visitors in from the doorstep.

Sunderland.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Wearside
s1loc: Sunderland is building a coastal visitor economy along the River Wear and the North Sea. The marquee draws include the National Glass Centre on the Wear's north bank, the Sunderland Museum and Winter Gardens, St Peter's Church at Monkwearmouth and the Blue Flag Roker and Seaburn beaches, with the Roker Pier and Lighthouse and the Davy lamp monument at the Stadium of Light marking the city's coal-mining heritage.

The leisure and activity layer is just as busy. The Stadium of Light hosts matches and arena concerts, while the Sunderland Empire Theatre, Mowbray Park, Herrington Country Park and the Seaburn seafront draw families. Stadium tours, the Sunderland Illuminations and Seaburn air and food festivals, plus the Bridges shopping quarter and the Keel Square public space, keep activity operators and event teams working across the season.

Heritage and hospitality round it out, from Penshaw Monument above Washington and Houghton le Spring to Washington Old Hall, the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust reserve at Washington and the Tommy statue and sea-glass beach at Seaham. A growing hotel trade runs through the city centre and the seafront, supported by local tour and guide operators, Sunderland station, the Tyne and Wear Metro and Newcastle Airport bringing visitors in from the doorstep.
